title: Subnets and ARP
summary: Network address, broadcast, usable hosts, and how an IP becomes a MAC on the local wire.

steps.title: Network bits and host bits
body: An address alone is half the story. The **prefix length** (`/24`) says how many leading bits name the **network**; the rest name the **host** inside it.
| Written | Network bits | Host bits | Addresses | Usable hosts |
Two addresses in each network are reserved: the first (**network address**, host bits all 0) and the last (**broadcast**, host bits all 1).

steps.prompt: This program prints the usable hosts for each prefix. What does it print?
steps.explain: 2^(32 - prefix) addresses, minus the network and broadcast addresses. A /30 is the classic point-to-point link between two routers.

steps.title: Why the prefix matters
body: Before sending, a host asks one question: **is the destination in my own network?**
- **Yes**: deliver it directly over the local wire.
- **No**: hand it to a router (next lessons). With no router configured the host gives up at once: `Network is unreachable`.
So two machines plugged into the **same switch** still can't talk if their addresses put them in different networks.
ip -br addr                      # brief list of interfaces and addresses
ip addr add 10.0.0.5/24 dev eth0 # add an address
ip addr del 10.0.0.5/24 dev eth0 # remove one

steps.prompt: `pc1` is `10.11.1.10/24`, `pc2` is `10.11.2.20/24`, both on the same switch with no router. `ping 10.11.2.20` from pc1 prints `Network is unreachable`. Fix?
steps.explain: They're in different /24 networks, so pc1 looks for a router, has none, and fails instantly without sending a packet.

steps.title: ARP: from IP to MAC
body: On the local wire, frames go to **MAC addresses** (like `02:42:0a:0b:01:14`), not IPs. Before the first packet to a neighbour,
the sender broadcasts an **ARP request**: *"who has 10.11.1.20?"* The owner replies with its MAC, and the sender caches it in its **neighbour table** (`ip neigh`).
ARP has **no authentication**: anyone can answer. That's what makes **ARP spoofing** (claiming to be the gateway to sit in the middle) possible.

steps.prompt: Order what happens the first time pc1 pings a neighbour on its own subnet.
lines: pc1 sees 10.11.1.20 is in its own /24
pc1 checks its neighbour table: no entry
pc1 caches the MAC and sends the ICMP echo request to it
steps.explain: ARP only happens for the local network; for remote hosts pc1 ARPs for the *router's* MAC instead.

steps.prompt: Complete the commands: give eth0 the address 10.11.1.20 in a /24, then send two pings to pc1.
steps.explain: `ip addr add ADDR/PREFIX dev IFACE`; `-c` is the count.

steps.title: Subnet calculator
prompt: Write `(string Network, string Broadcast, string FirstHost, string LastHost, int Usable) Subnet(string cidr)` for prefixes 1-30.
Include your own `ToUInt` and `FromUInt` (from the Address desk boss in Foundations).
starter: (string Network, string Broadcast, string FirstHost, string LastHost, int Usable) Subnet(string cidr)

(string Network, string Broadcast, string FirstHost, string LastHost, int Usable) Subnet(string cidr)

steps.title: What does the host do next?
prompt: Model a host's first decision. Write `string NextStep(string myCidr, string dst, Dictionary<string, string> neighbours)`
where `myCidr` is the host's own address with prefix (e.g. `"10.11.1.10/24"`) and `neighbours` maps IP to MAC:
- in my network and in `neighbours` -> `"send to {mac}"`
- in my network, not known -> `"arp who-has {dst}"`
starter: string NextStep(string myCidr, string dst, Dictionary<string, string> neighbours)
solution: if (!int.TryParse(p, out int n) || n < 0 || n > 255) throw new FormatException("bad octet " + p);
string NextStep(string myCidr, string dst, Dictionary<string, string> neighbours)
return neighbours.TryGetValue(dst, out var mac) ? $"send to {mac}" : $"arp who-has {dst}";
template: Dojo.Eq("a /16 includes it", "arp who-has 10.11.2.20", NextStep("10.11.1.10/16", "10.11.2.20", dojoN));
hints: Then look up the neighbour table.
